chunks: When he knows that the obligation of religious duties remains upon him and that the Imam is in occultation from him, he discerns that it is because of a matter that refers back to himself, as our group says regarding one who did not contemplate the path to the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and thus did not attain knowledge: it becomes obligatory for him to be certain that he did not attain it due to a shortcoming that refers back to himself; otherwise, it would be obligatory to remove the obligation from him, even if he does not know in what specific matter his shortcoming occurred.

key_terms.اسْتِتَار: Occultation or concealment (specifically of the Imam)
key_terms.تَقْصِير: Shortcoming, negligence, or failure to fulfill a duty
key_terms.تَكْلِيف: Religious obligation or duty imposed by God

ai.seo_question: Why are religious duties still obligatory during the Imam's occultation if one lacks certainty in God?
ai.summary: Al-Tusi articulates the principle of *istishab al-taklif* (presumption of continued obligation), arguing that the Imam's hiddenness does not suspend religious duties but rather shifts the burden of proof to the individual. This ensures that the faithful remain accountable for their spiritual state, attributing any lack of certainty to personal negligence rather than divine concealment, a cornerstone of Usuli jurisprudence during the Major Occultation.
